Definition: Percentage of the national population covered by at least one 4G/LTE mobile network signal, whether or not they subscribe to the service. 4G is the practical minimum for meaningful broadband connectivity enabling digital services.
Comments: ITU Digital Development Dashboard indicates population covered by at least a 4G mobile network = 70% (2022), mapping to 50–74% bracket.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: MACRA regulatory data reported via Ecofin Agency (8 Oct 2025) shows 4G population coverage reached 75.1% by Q3 2024, up from the 70% (2022) ITU DDD figure used originally. This moves the score from the 50-74% bracket to 75-89%; upgraded to code 4.

Definition: Affordability of mobile broadband data, measured as the cost of a basic mobile data plan (1-2GB) as a percentage of GNI per capita. The UN Broadband Commission target is below 2% of monthly GNI per capita. Affordability is the single largest barrier to internet adoption in Africa.
Comments: ITU Digital Development Dashboard reports 'Mobile broadband basket as a % of GNI p.c.' = 9.4% (2022), which falls in 5–10% bracket.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: No fresher country-specific ITU Price Basket figure for Malawi could be located beyond the 2022 DDD figure (9.4% of GNI p.c.). ITU's 2023 global affordability report confirms a general downward trend in mobile-broadband basket costs across Africa but no updated Malawi-specific percentage was found in the sources checked. Confirmed at code 2 (5-10%) pending a more current national figure.

Definition: Percentage of individuals who used the internet (from any location, via any device) in the last three months. This measures actual internet adoption beyond network availability, capturing the combined effect of infrastructure, affordability, digital literacy, and relevance.
Comments: ITU Digital Development Dashboard shows individuals using the Internet = 28% in 2022.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Recent sources give internet-user estimates for Malawi ranging from 18% (ITU 2023, cited via MACRA/Ecofin Oct 2025) and 17.99% (World Bank, 2023) to 27.7% (Afrobarometer Dec 2025, citing UNDP 2025). All fall within the 15-29% bracket, so the original score is confirmed despite the spread in underlying estimates.

Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
Comments: ITU Digital Development Dashboard lists international bandwidth per Internet user = 13 kbit/s (2022), which falls in 5–19 kbit/s bracket.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: No more recent international-bandwidth-per-user figure for Malawi was found in the sources checked (Network Readiness Index and Internet Society Pulse pages did not give a directly comparable updated figure). The ITU DDD 2022 figure of 13 kbit/s per user (5-19 kbit/s bracket) remains the best available authoritative estimate. Confirmed at code 2.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
Comments: DataReportal (using GSMA Intelligence) reports 14.1M mobile connections, equivalent to 63.0% of population (Oct/late 2025), mapping to 55–69% bracket.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original comment's own arithmetic was inconsistent (states 63% maps to the 55-69% bracket but then applies code 3 = 40-54%). The 63% DataReportal/GSMA figure is total cellular connections, not unique subscribers; MACRA's regulatory survey covering 2023 (via Telecompaper) found 42% of mobile users hold multiple active SIMs, so adjusting connections for SIM multiplicity implies unique-subscriber penetration of roughly 40-45%, consistent with a 2019 GSMA Digital Identity report estimate of 30% unique subscriber penetration and plausible subsequent growth. Confirmed at code 3 (40-54%); comment corrected to avoid conflating connections with unique subscribers.

Definition: Percentage of mobile connections using smartphones (as opposed to feature phones or basic phones). Smartphones are the minimum device requirement for accessing most digital public infrastructure services, apps, and mobile internet.
Comments: 90.1% broadband mobile connections proxy for 60-79% smartphones
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original code used '90.1% mobile broadband connections' (i.e. 3G/4G/5G network technology) as a proxy for smartphone adoption, which conflates connection technology with handset type - GSMA explicitly warns this 'broadband' figure should not be read as a device-type proxy. The US Government's Malawi Digital Economy country commercial guide (trade.gov, 2026) cites smartphone ownership at 36.3%, consistent with FinScope Consumer Malawi 2023 finding only 54% of adults own any phone at all (basic or smart) and with Malawi likely sitting below the roughly 42% Sub-Saharan Africa regional average for smartphone adoption (GSMA Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa 2023). Downgraded from code 4 (60-79%) to code 2 (20-39%); recommend human review to confirm against a primary GSMA Intelligence country-level figure if available.

Definition: The proportion of the population with basic digital skills (ability to use a computer, smartphone, or the internet for simple tasks such as sending messages, finding information, or using apps). Based on ITU household survey data, Afrobarometer, or national ICT surveys.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original score used internet-user share (18%) as a proxy for digital literacy, but two more directly relevant sources give much higher and mutually inconsistent figures: the PPPC/EY Digital Skills Ecosystem and Gap Assessment (Malawi, 2021) found 44% of the population possesses foundational digital skills, while Afrobarometer (Dec 2025, citing UNDP 2025) cites a national digital literacy rate of 62%. Both are well above the current 10-24% bracket but disagree on whether the true figure sits in the 40-59% or 60%+ bracket. Revised provisionally to code 4 (40-59%, the more directly-measured of the two figures), but flagged for human review to resolve the conflict between sources before finalising.
